### Arrival in New York

After his ordination in the summer of 1915, it was time for Dick to spread his wings and be given a flock to tend. The problem was where. Ireland was factory for priests, producing far more than it could employ, and there was certainly no space for him at home in mid-Waterford, had he wanted to return home. Thus, a posting abroad was the obvious solution because English-speaking Catholic populations were exploding in Britain, the USA and the Antipodes. A few years later, Dick's younger brother Rennie would move to Lancashire where there was a huge Irish community, while Dick's correspondence shows him in touch with priests in Australia, a mix of people he had studied with or under during his youth.

It's not clear why exactly New York was chosen for Dick but perhaps the size of the city with its myriad opportunities made it an attractive or appropriate location, for a man of his talents. New York had been undergoing enormous amounts of immigration and the Catholic groups were mostly from Irish, Italian, German, Polish, and other Eastern European backgrounds, making the city known as the "Immigrant Archdiocese". A church's congregation might be composed mostly of one particular language group but on Sunday morning that wouldn't matter as mass itself was delivered in Latin, and would remain so for the remainder of Dick's life. But in those days, the parish was deeply integrated into the community, with no shortage of activities throughout the week so it made sense for Dick to join up with the Irish diaspora. One curiosity of the New York melting pot was that Catholic numbers were not growing as fast as immigration because the city was experiencing an exodus of its middle-class to the suburbs, leaving the parishes in need of leaders and the archdiocese in need of consolidation.

Dick was posted to St Boniface's Church in Turtle Bay, Manhatten, on what is now the grounds of the UN Headquarters. The church had begun life as a German-speaking congregation in the mid-nineteenth century and later spent some decades as a bi-lingual congregation. But by the time Dick arrived, it was predominantly Irish with a recent surge in the number of Italian congregants, and this shift was important given that the Great War had begun and Dick would soon be saying farewell to parishioners heading off to Europe to fight Germany.

<https://www.dib.ie/biography/farley-john-murphy-a3004>

Dick was appointed as assistant pastor to Fr Francis Xavier E Albert (**explain more)** while the Archbishop of New York was Cardinal John Farley, an Armagh man who grew up during the famine before emigrating to New York in 1864, in his twenty-second year. He completed his education in New York, entered the priesthood as a seminarian, but was ordained in Rome, a move that would prove vital for the culmination of his career. Farley was appointed Cardinal to the Pope in 1911 and kept the position until his death in 1919. He was famous for consolidating the archdiocese, in the face of so much social change, and morphing it into powerful civic and religious force within the city. His work would be indirectly helpful to the Irish revolutionary cause as the decade progressed because the unity of the archdiocese allowed for an existing network of closely-connected believers to transpose their focus from religion to politics while maintaining and even strengthening their bonds as a community.

### **Work in the parish**

`"He is one of the finest young priests I have ever come across and all the parishioners are simply crazy about him."`

While Farley pieced together the jigsaw of New Yorkes, Dick's role on the ground involved getting people in to mass and ideally to get involved in the many other community activities that the church was involved in. There was no better man for the job than Dick, fresh off the boat. He quickly began going round the houses, knocking door to door and having a word with anyone who had stopped attending mass regularly. Within two months, he doubled the church-going attendance of one sodality and trebled that of another. It was said that there was "not an idle bone in the man's body". That does not mean that he doubled or even trebled the entire congregation; instead the focus was on increasing the numbers of particular subgroups in the parish.

Dick became heavily involved as a spiritual director of the Holy Name Society, a confraternity of laymen that had a strong presence across America at the time. The society promoted social cohesion among male parishioners, moral discipline and temperance, often with processions accompanied by music. When Dick arrived, members would meet monthly but he seems to have been a major galvanising force. He worked hard to get meeting rooms for the men and within a couple of years they had a place to go "every evening of the week and every week of the year". The meeting rooms would become a refuge where they could play music, read books from their library, play billiards or just have a place to sit and write their daily correspondence, free from the cramped conditions that many of them would have lived in, with large families and noisy neighbours. It was perhaps no surprise that by the time Dick left, the membership had quintupled in the St Boniface Holy Name Society, including a significant junior branch, and membership may well have been even greater if men had not died in the war. However, America would join the war until April 1917, which meant that Dick could focus first on his major passion – music.

When America entered the war in the spring of 1917, there was a major dearth in volunteers, and there were just ten men from the parish willing to volunteer. We have them photographed with Dick and the Parish Priest, Fr Francis Xavier Albert, looking sprightly and gay, ready for their adventure, presumably unaware of the horrors that awaited them. The rest of the community must have been a little more savvy as volunteer numbers were low until men were drafted, and in total 293 members of the Boniface parish were sent off to risk their lives in the pursuit of European freedom. #### **Slides & Early lectures**

Ireland

We saw in the last post that The Very Reverand Monsignor Richard J Casey amassed a sizeable collection of slides from talks he gave during his time in New York (1915-20) and then afterwards in Ireland during the early years of The Fres State. Their subject matter, the venues and the newspaper reports, mostly based on newspaper clippings that Casey kept, but also based on more general research into the topic of funding drives in America.

    -   The slides that Casey chose portray a land of "emerald hills, the castles of ancient prestige, as well as the modern cities, towns, people and social customs of the old land', according to one contemporary newspaper report. We have a map of the unpartitioned island, some shrivelled up shamrocks, and meticulously preserved castles dating from an ancient time that must have seemed barely fathomable to his New World audience. There's The Rock of Cashel, a round tower on Devinish Island in Fermanagh, and the rope bridge near the Giant's Causeway. Casey includes some images of County Watarford, including the Historic Town of Lismore, Reginald's Tower in Waterford City, and his own parish church in Dungarvan. There's an image of a thatched cottage and one (I didn't see) of Croagh Patrick, a pilgrimage site. There's a notable lack of barren wild landscapes of the kind Americans like to visit nowadays (e.g. the Ring of Kerry, The Burren, Donegal, etc). There is one of Kilkee in West Clare but I see it either so I don't know if it's a photo of the town or the nearby landscapes.

-   One such name was The Gaelic Society, and by January 1919, Casey was presenting at one of their céilidhthe, a combination that shows how revolutionary fervour could be drummed up amidst a cultural event, and a reminder that the Irish cultural revolution really holds primacy over the political revolution.

It is interesting to note Casey's choice of rebels and reformers. One slide shows Wolfe Tone, who led the failed rebellion of 1798. Another shows the Wicklow Parliamentarian, Charles Stewart Parnell, his deceased body lying in state. Finally, there is bronze statue of [Fr William Casey](https://www.dib.ie/biography/casey-william-a1544) in Abbeyfeale, Co. Limerick, the "peoples' priest". This Casey – who is also no relation to our subject – must have functioned as quite the role model for our Richard. He was a Gaelgeoir, a musician, a GAA man, and temperance activist, which I suspect Fr Richard was too. Fr William was most active in the Land League, for which he gained huge local support, and so too was Fr Richard's uncle – another Fr Richard J Casey – to whom I shall one day return. There are no slides related to the Fenian Uprising of 1867, even though its veteran John Devoy had become the leading Republican in New York by the time of Casey's lectures. This may be because the Fenians tried to keep a low profile and used codenames for their gatherings. Plus the audience may simply have been familiar with Devoy or the recently-deceased O'Donovan Rossa, and would thus have had no need to slides of them.

#### Revolutionary Groups

-   

-   **Friends of Irish Freedom (FOIF)** was founded in 1916 as a broad-based Irish-American nationalist group. It was closely aligned with **Clan na Gael** and supported the 1916 Rising and Irish independence. FOIF raised **over \$350,000** for Irish causes through the Irish Relief Fund [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friends_of_Irish_Freedom).

    -   ![](images/clipboard-2240131029.png)

-   **American Committee for Relief in Ireland (ACRI)** was formed in **1920** to provide humanitarian aid during the War of Independence. It focused on **non-political relief**, but many of its members were sympathetic to the nationalist cause [Cambridge University Press & Assessment](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/irish-historical-studies/article/abs/american-committee-for-relief-in-ireland-192022/23909DF7F637B7F3FBF6FB8E7234A64D) [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/stable/30008232?read-now=1).

-   **Tensions arose** between FOIF and ACRI over control of funds and messaging. FOIF wanted to ensure money supported independence, while ACRI emphasized neutrality and humanitarian aid. This led to **splits in Irish-American support networks**, especially in New York.

### **Bringing his car home, June 1920**

IMG_20251106_115114.jpg

Moving his car home to Ireland, June 14, 1920 (after this date)

Moore & McCormack steamship agents!

**One of the greatest curiosities of the RJC's return home from New York was that he had his car boxed up and sent home in advance of his own departure. It is not clear exactly why RJC had his own car as it was still unusual for a priest to have his own vehicle, especially in a densely-packed city such as New York. A parish church might own a car for use among its priests, but not usually the priests themselves. Car ownership would have been more common among rural priests with need to cover greater distances. It is thus a marker of how financially savvy RJC must have been, although questions might be asked of how he amassed the cash needed for a vehicle of his own. Obviously it would be an unfair and huge jump to connect his personal wealth to the fact that he was involved in fundraising throughout his time in New York, although that hardly simplified his finances. We must remember that he grew up in a family of shopkeepers who must have kept close tabs on all finances - daily, weekly, annual – while, being the eldest in the family, RJC must have been well trained by his father.**

Tax Letter 1918 IMG_20251106_115945.jpg from Farley

March 19, 1918

Rev Richard gets a letter about Federal tax payments. Why?

From the Archbishop of New York, John Cardinal Farley

**It is worth noting that the scrapbook contains a lengthy letter from the Archbishop of New York, John Cardinal Farley, advising pastors on how to keep their finances in order. Modern readers will be astonished to know that only 2% Federal Tax was being charged on higher earners, with a further new deduction of 2% due to the War Revenue Act, although this was graded higher for higher earners.**

**So while we details may not all be clear, we do know that RJC was not afraid to drive a bargain and ask for a discounted rate. His car was shipped home at half price because the shipping company, Moore and McCormack were willing to oblige and even go out of their way. Normally, they seem to have been shipping government goods, including various kinds of boxed up vessels, but these were not their own boats so they couldn't control the rates. However, the *Nyanza* was a steamboat owned and operated by the company itself, sailing directly from** **Brooklyn to Dublin, where he would live for the rest of his life.**

**Moving home must have been bittersweet for Casey, a situation that is elequently mirrored through the tears and and smiles of his very close friend, Patrick J McNamara of the Military Band and Orchestra, with whom RJC worked very closely throughout his time in New York. McNamara was so happy to hear from his very close friend but was clearly sad at losing such a close working partner, and of course back then it was not clear if or when friends across the pond would see each other again. As for RJC, the sweetness is two-fold, coming from the simple joy of being home on the auld sod, but also from the enormous political developments of the day. McNamara's letter was sent just two days after the truce and ceasefire between Irish and British sides. Thus he makes reference to the 'newly free and happy Ireland' in which RJC was now living, and neither could have known that it was a condition that was sadly not to last. Yet there must have been deep sadness for RJC at giving up on so much that he had developed in his energetic years in New York. For McNamara, the focus is in music, the basis of their relationship, and he notes that St Boniface's parish have had no entrants to the Feis Ceoil since RJC departed, while they were winning gold and silver medals while he was there. It is not so much the musical ability of RJC which is missed here, but his rousing qualities, getting students enthused so that professionals like McNamara could get them up to the level required.**

**For RJC, his return home feels like the begining of the end for him. It is as though something died in him. The vivacity reduces**

#### **Slides & Early lectures**

We saw in the last post that The Very Reverand Monsignor Richard J Casey amassed a sizeable collection of slides from talks he gave during his time in New York (1915-20) and then afterwards in Ireland during the early years of The Fres State. Their subject matter, the venues and the newspaper reports, mostly based on newspaper clippings that Casey kept, but also based on more general research into the topic of funding drives in America.

    -   The slides that Casey chose portray a land of "emerald hills, the castles of ancient prestige, as well as the modern cities, towns, people and social customs of the old land', according to one contemporary newspaper report. We have a map of the unpartitioned island, some shrivelled up shamrocks, and meticulously preserved castles dating from an ancient time that must have seemed barely fathomable to his New World audience. There's The Rock of Cashel, a round tower on Devinish Island in Fermanagh, and the rope bridge near the Giant's Causeway. Casey includes some images of County Watarford, including the Historic Town of Lismore, Reginald's Tower in Waterford City, and his own parish church in Dungarvan. There's an image of a thatched cottage and one (I didn't see) of Croagh Patrick, a pilgrimage site. There's a notable lack of barren wild landscapes of the kind Americans like to visit nowadays (e.g. the Ring of Kerry, The Burren, Donegal, etc). There is one of Kilkee in West Clare but I see it either so I don't know if it's a photo of the town or the nearby landscapes.

-   One such name was The Gaelic Society, and by January 1919, Casey was presenting at one of their céilidhthe, a combination that shows how revolutionary fervour could be drummed up amidst a cultural event, and a reminder that the Irish cultural revolution really holds primacy over the political revolution.

It is interesting to note Casey's choice of rebels and reformers. One slide shows Wolfe Tone, who led the failed rebellion of 1798. Another shows the Wicklow Parliamentarian, Charles Stewart Parnell, his deceased body lying in state. Finally, there is bronze statue of [Fr William Casey](https://www.dib.ie/biography/casey-william-a1544) in Abbeyfeale, Co. Limerick, the "peoples' priest". This Casey – who is also no relation to our subject – must have functioned as quite the role model for our Richard. He was a Gaelgeoir, a musician, a GAA man, and temperance activist, which I suspect Fr Richard was too. Fr William was most active in the Land League, for which he gained huge local support, and so too was Fr Richard's uncle – another Fr Richard J Casey – to whom I shall one day return. There are no slides related to the Fenian Uprising of 1867, even though its veteran John Devoy had become the leading Republican in New York by the time of Casey's lectures. This may be because the Fenians tried to keep a low profile and used codenames for their gatherings. Plus the audience may simply have been familiar with Devoy or the recently-deceased O'Donovan Rossa, and would thus have had no need to slides of them.

Among the revolutionary fervour, there are slides of Wolfe Tone who led the failed rebellion of 1798, Parnell's body lying in state, and the bronze statue of [Fr William Casey](https://www.dib.ie/biography/casey-william-a1544) in Abbeyfeale, Co. Limerick. This Casey – who is no relation to our subject – must have been quite the role model for our Richard. He was a Gaelgeoir, musician, GAA man, and temperance activist, which I suspect Fr Richard was too. There are no slides related to the Fenian Uprising of 1867, even though its veteran John Devoy had become the leading Republican in New York by the time of Casey's lectures. In my next post, we will see that Casey's talks may have been part of a series of covert funding campaigns for the Revolution.. For example. one 1919 soirée saw both a céilidhe and Casey's (music-filled) presentation. It was held by the Gaelic Society in New York. We shall also see newspaper reports of how Casey's was not afraid to include his thoughts on the English oppressors of the Irish people.

#### Revolutionary Groups

-   

-   **Friends of Irish Freedom (FOIF)** was founded in 1916 as a broad-based Irish-American nationalist group. It was closely aligned with **Clan na Gael** and supported the 1916 Rising and Irish independence. FOIF raised **over \$350,000** for Irish causes through the Irish Relief Fund [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friends_of_Irish_Freedom).

    -   ![](images/clipboard-2240131029.png)

-   **American Committee for Relief in Ireland (ACRI)** was formed in **1920** to provide humanitarian aid during the War of Independence. It focused on **non-political relief**, but many of its members were sympathetic to the nationalist cause [Cambridge University Press & Assessment](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/irish-historical-studies/article/abs/american-committee-for-relief-in-ireland-192022/23909DF7F637B7F3FBF6FB8E7234A64D) [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/stable/30008232?read-now=1).

-   **Tensions arose** between FOIF and ACRI over control of funds and messaging. FOIF wanted to ensure money supported independence, while ACRI emphasized neutrality and humanitarian aid. This led to **splits in Irish-American support networks**, especially in New York.

### **Bringing his car home, June 1920**

IMG_20251106_115114.jpg

Moving his car home to Ireland, June 14, 1920 (after this date)

Moore & McCormack steamship agents!

**One of the greatest curiosities of the RJC's return home from New York was that he had his car boxed up and sent home in advance of his own departure. It is not clear exactly why RJC had his own car as it was still unusual for a priest to have his own vehicle, especially in a densely-packed city such as New York. A parish church might own a car for use among its priests, but not usually the priests themselves. Car ownership would have been more common among rural priests with need to cover greater distances. It is thus a marker of how financially savvy RJC must have been, although questions might be asked of how he amassed the cash needed for a vehicle of his own. Obviously it would be an unfair and huge jump to connect his personal wealth to the fact that he was involved in fundraising throughout his time in New York, although that hardly simplified his finances. We must remember that he grew up in a family of shopkeepers who must have kept close tabs on all finances - daily, weekly, annual – while, being the eldest in the family, RJC must have been well trained by his father.**

Tax Letter 1918 IMG_20251106_115945.jpg from Farley

March 19, 1918

Rev Richard gets a letter about Federal tax payments. Why?

From the Archbishop of New York, John Cardinal Farley

**It is worth noting that the scrapbook contains a lengthy letter from the Archbishop of New York, John Cardinal Farley, advising pastors on how to keep their finances in order. Modern readers will be astonished to know that only 2% Federal Tax was being charged on higher earners, with a further new deduction of 2% due to the War Revenue Act, although this was graded higher for higher earners.**

**So while we details may not all be clear, we do know that RJC was not afraid to drive a bargain and ask for a discounted rate. His car was shipped home at half price because the shipping company, Moore and McCormack were willing to oblige and even go out of their way. Normally, they seem to have been shipping government goods, including various kinds of boxed up vessels, but these were not their own boats so they couldn't control the rates. However, the *Nyanza* was a steamboat owned and operated by the company itself, sailing directly from** **Brooklyn to Dublin, where he would live for the rest of his life.**
